_source: AI-drafted per book (2026-07-21 fan-out), adversarially verified by a second model; 19 boundary corrections after verification; 2 boundaries senior-adjudicated. John's editorial layer remains scene-boundary-overrides.json.
_semantics: One entry per scene start (scenes staging truth) except each book's first scene (auto-anchored at offset 0 by stage1_pope). n = the scene's first Greek vulgate line; anchor = verbatim text from the emitted Pope book text, must occur exactly once in its book and begin at a verse-line start. Scene-boundary edits in apparatus staging will fail stage1 loudly until this dataset is updated to match.

anchors.anchor: Now at their native realms the Greeks arrived;
anchors.note: New paragraph after the proem's close, opening the narrative proper with the Greeks' homecoming and Ulysses' detention by Calypso.

anchors.anchor: But now the god, remote, a heavenly guest,
anchors.note: Marks the pivot from the Greeks'-homecoming narration to Poseidon's absence in Ethiopia and the ensuing Olympian council, matching Murray's 'save Poseidon... had gone among the far-off Ethiopians.'

anchors.anchor: Here paused the god; and pensive thus replies
anchors.note: Pope compresses Zeus's whole Aegisthus speech into one block (43-56); this is the transition to Minerva's plea for Odysseus that Murray's line 44 (mid-speech) leads into.

anchors.anchor: “Father and king adored!” Minerva cried,
anchors.note: Opens Minerva's second speech (after Zeus's assent), which proposes sending Hermes to Ogygia -- matches Murray's repeated 'Father of us all... let us send forth Hermes.'

anchors.anchor: From high Olympus prone her flight she bends,
anchors.note: Begins Athena's actual descent to Ithaca (after the prior scene's arming/proposal), matching Murray's 'Then she went darting down from the heights of Olympus.'

anchors.anchor: Thus affable and mild, the prince precedes,
anchors.note: Follows directly on Telemachus's welcoming words and begins his leading the disguised goddess indoors, matching Murray's 'So saying, he led the way, and Pallas Athena followed.'

anchors.anchor: Meanwhile, in whispers to his heavenly guest
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's private aside to his guest, matching Murray's 'Telemachus spoke to flashing-eyed Athena, holding his head close, that the others might not hear.'

anchors.anchor: “My birth I boast (the blue-eyed virgin cries)
anchors.note: Opens Mentes's reply giving her lineage and affirming Odysseus's return, matching Murray's 'I declare that I am Mentes, the son of wise Anchialus.'

anchors.anchor: “To prove a genuine birth (the prince replies)
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's answer questioning his own parentage, matching Murray's 'My mother says that I am his child; but I know not.'

anchors.anchor: With tender pity touch’d, the goddess cried:
anchors.note: Opens the goddess's long exhortation (which later specifies the assembly and the voyage to Pylos and Sparta), matching Murray's Athena replying in anger/pity to Telemachus's lament.

anchors.anchor: “The counsel of my friend (the youth rejoin’d)
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's grateful reply that leads into his offer of a parting gift, matching Murray's 'Stranger, in truth thou speakest these things with kindly thought... bearing a gift.'

anchors.anchor: Then first he recognized the ethereal guest;
anchors.note: Follows immediately on Athena's bird-departure and opens Telemachus's realization and rejoining of the suitors to hear Phemius's song, matching Murray's 'in his heart she put strength and courage... he went among the wooers.'

anchors.anchor: Meantime, rekindled at the royal charms,
anchors.note: Opens the suitors' uproar of desire for Penelope that Telemachus interrupts to assert himself, matching Murray's 'the wooers broke into uproar... wise Telemachus was the first to speak.'

anchors.anchor: Meantime the lyre rejoins the sprightly lay;
anchors.note: Follows Telemachus's evasive answer to Eurymachus and opens the closing dance-and-feast-until-evening passage, matching Murray's 'the wooers turned to the dance and to gladsome song... waited till evening.'

anchors.anchor: ’Twas silence all. At last AEgyptius spoke;
anchors.note: Opens Aegyptius's speech to the assembled peers, matching Murray's 'the lord Aegyptius was the first to speak.'

anchors.anchor: He spoke. Telemachus with transport glows,
anchors.note: Marks Telemachus rising to take the floor after Aegyptius, matching Murray's 'the dear son of Odysseus rejoiced at the word of omen... was fain to speak.'

anchors.anchor: While thus he spoke, with rage and grief he frown’d,
anchors.note: Narrates Telemachus dashing down his staff in tears, immediately preceding Antinous's answer, matching Murray's 'Thus he spoke in wrath, and dashed the staff down upon the ground, bursting into tears.'

anchors.anchor: While yet he speaks, Telemachus replies:
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's answer to Antinous's shroud-story speech, matching Murray's 'wise Telemachus answered him.'

anchors.anchor: With that, two eagles from a mountain’s height
anchors.note: Opens the eagle-omen episode directly, matching Murray's 'Zeus... sent forth two eagles, flying from on high.'

anchors.anchor: To whom Eurymachus—“Fly, dotard fly,
anchors.note: Opens Eurymachus's dismissive reply to Halitherses's prophecy, matching Murray's 'Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered him.'

anchors.anchor: To whom the youth: “Since then in vain I tell
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's reply to Eurymachus, which goes on to request a ship for Pylos and Sparta, matching Murray's 'give me a swift ship.'

anchors.anchor: He ceased; and while abash’d the peers attend,
anchors.note: Introduces Mentor rising to speak after Telemachus's request, matching Murray's 'among them rose Mentor.'

anchors.anchor: Then, with a rushing sound the assembly bend
anchors.note: Narrates the assembly breaking up and Telemachus going apart to the shore, matching Murray's 'he hastily broke up the assembly... Telemachus went apart to the shore of the sea.'

anchors.anchor: She spoke: to his high dome the prince returns,
anchors.note: Follows Mentor/Athena's promise of a ship and narrates Telemachus's return home to the mocking Antinous, matching Murray's 'nor did Telemachus tarry long... but went his way to the house.'

anchors.anchor: He spoke and frown’d, nor longer deign’d to stay,
anchors.note: Follows Telemachus's retort to Antinous and opens the suitors' private mockery, matching Murray's 'he snatched his hand from the hand of Antinous... they mocked and jeered at him.'

anchors.anchor: Meantime the lofty rooms the prince surveys,
anchors.note: Opens the storeroom scene directly, matching Murray's 'Telemachus went down to the high-roofed treasure-chamber of his father.'

anchors.anchor: “Far hence (replied the prince) thy fears be driven:
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's reply reassuring Eurycleia and asking her oath of silence, matching Murray's 'wise Telemachus answered her... swear to tell naught of this to my dear mother.'

anchors.anchor: Telemachus already press’d the shore;
anchors.note: Narrates Telemachus stepping ashore with Mentor/Athena leading, immediately preceding her admonishment, matching Murray's 'Forth too from the ship stepped Telemachus, and Athena led the way.'

anchors.anchor: To whom the martial goddess thus rejoin’d:
anchors.note: Opens Athena's reassuring second reply to Telemachus's admission of shyness, which then leads them onward to the Pylian gathering, matching Murray's 'the goddess, flashing-eyed Athena, answered him.'

anchors.anchor: Then first approaching to the elder guest,
anchors.note: Opens Pisistratus's address to the disguised Athena asking her to pray first, matching Murray's 'he spoke to Pallas Athena... Pray now, stranger, to the lord Poseidon.'

anchors.anchor: The banquet done, the narrative old man,
anchors.note: Opens Nestor's turn to speak after the feast, matching Murray's 'the horseman, Nestor of Gerenia, spoke first among them.'

anchors.anchor: To him experienced Nestor thus rejoin’d:
anchors.note: Opens Nestor's reply to Telemachus's question about his father, matching Murray's 'the horseman, Nestor of Gerenia, answered him.'

anchors.anchor: Then Discord, sent by Pallas from above,
anchors.note: Marks the pivot to Athena's strife between the sons of Atreus, matching Murray's 'through the fell wrath of the flashing-eyed goddess... for she caused strife between the two sons of Atreus.'

anchors.anchor: The fourth day shone, when all their labours o’er,
anchors.note: Opens the account of Nestor's own safe, separate voyage home to Pylos, matching Murray's 'It was the fourth day when in Argos the company of Diomedes... stayed their shapely ships; but I held on toward Pylos.'

anchors.anchor: Thus he; and Nestor took the word: “My son,
anchors.note: Opens Nestor's question about the suitors afflicting Telemachus's house, matching Murray's 'the horseman, Nestor of Gerenia, answered him... many wooers for the hand of thy mother devise evils.'

anchors.anchor: Thus check’d, replied Ulysses’ prudent heir:
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's reply that pivots the conversation to ask Nestor directly how Agamemnon died, matching Murray's 'wise Telemachus answered her... Mentor, no longer let us tell of these things.'

anchors.anchor: “Meantime from flaming Troy we cut the way
anchors.note: Marks the pivot from Nestor's account of Aegisthus's seduction/murder to the separate account of Menelaus's storm-driven voyage, matching Murray's 'Now we were sailing together on our way from Troy, the son of Atreus and I.'

anchors.anchor: Thus while he speaks the ruddy sun descends,
anchors.note: Marks the sunset that closes Nestor's long narration and introduces Athena's proposal, matching Murray's 'the sun set, and darkness came on. Then among them spoke the goddess, flashing-eyed Athena.'

anchors.anchor: “Well hast thou spoke (the blue-eyed maid replies),
anchors.note: Opens Athena's answer to Nestor's insistence on hosting them, in which she defers Telemachus's lodging to Nestor, matching Murray's 'the goddess, flashing-eyed Athena, answered him: Well indeed hast thou spoken in this, old friend.'

anchors.anchor: Then, turning with the word, Minerva flies,
anchors.note: Narrates Athena's departure as a sea-eagle immediately before Nestor's amazed prayer, matching Murray's 'she departed in the likeness of a sea-eagle; and amazement fell upon all at the sight.'

anchors.anchor: When now Aurora, daughter of the dawn,
anchors.note: Opens the dawn formula introducing Nestor's rising and the day's preparations, matching Murray's 'Soon as early Dawn appeared, the rosy-fingered, up from his bed rose the horseman, Nestor of Gerenia.'

anchors.anchor: To these the senior thus declared his will:
anchors.note: Opens Nestor's instructions for the sacrifice to Athena, matching Murray's 'Come now, let one go to the plain for a heifer... let one bid the goldsmith Laerces come hither.'

anchors.anchor: While these officious tend the rites divine,
anchors.note: Opens the couplet introducing Polycaste's bathing of Telemachus, matching Murray's 'the fair Polycaste, the youngest daughter of Nestor... bathed Telemachus.'

anchors.anchor: The glittering seat Telemachus ascends;
anchors.note: Opens the departure-by-chariot passage, matching Murray's 'to the plain, and left the steep citadel of Pylos. So all day long they shook the yoke.'

anchors.anchor: “Insensate! (with a sigh the king replies,)
anchors.note: Opens Menelaus's rebuke of Eteoneus and order to welcome the strangers, matching Murray's 'stirred to sore displeasure, fair-haired Menelaus spoke to him.'

anchors.anchor: Sufficed, soft whispering thus to Nestor’s son,
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's private aside to Pisistratus marveling at the palace, matching Murray's 'Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor, holding his head close to him, that the others might not hear.'

anchors.anchor: In this suspense bright Helen graced the room;
anchors.note: Opens Helen's entrance, matching Murray's 'forth then from her fragrant high-roofed chamber came Helen, like Artemis of the golden arrows.'

anchors.anchor: “See there confess’d (Pisistratus replies)
anchors.note: Opens Pisistratus's confirmation of Telemachus's identity, matching Murray's 'Then Peisistratus, son of Nestor, answered him.'

anchors.anchor: He ceased; a gush of grief began to rise:
anchors.note: Opens the shared weeping that follows Menelaus's lament, matching Murray's 'in them all aroused the desire of lament. Argive Helen wept... Telemachus wept, and Menelaus.'

anchors.anchor: He said, Asphalion swift the laver brings;
anchors.note: Opens the return to the feast and Helen's drug in the wine, matching Murray's 'Asphalion poured water over their hands... Then Helen, daughter of Zeus, took other counsel.'

anchors.anchor: “Right well (replied the king) your speech displays
anchors.note: Opens Menelaus's reply to Helen's story, which pivots into his own Wooden Horse recollection, matching Murray's 'fair-haired Menelaus answered her and said.'

anchors.anchor: Soon as the morn, in orient purple dress’d,
anchors.note: Opens the dawn formula that leads directly into Menelaus rising and questioning Telemachus, matching Murray's 'Soon as early Dawn appeared, the rosy-fingered, up from his bed arose Menelaus.'

anchors.anchor: “O highly-favour’d delegate of Jove!
anchors.note: Opens Telemachus's reply to Menelaus's question, explaining the suitors' ravaging and requesting news of Odysseus, matching Murray's request that closes this speech before Menelaus's angry reply.

anchors.anchor: “Long on the Egyptian coast by calms confined,
anchors.note: Opens Menelaus's Egypt narrative proper, matching Murray's 'In Egypt, eager though I was to journey hither, the gods still held me back.'

anchors.anchor: She ceased, and bounding from the shelfy shore,
anchors.note: Marks the end of Eidothea's spoken instructions and the resumption of Menelaus's own narration of carrying out the ambush, matching the shift from counsel to execution.

anchors.anchor: Vain efforts with superior power compress’d,
anchors.note: Opens the moment Proteus, spent from shape-shifting, questions Menelaus, matching Murray's 'when at last that old man, skilled in wizard arts, grew weary, then he questioned me.'

anchors.anchor: “By Juno’s guardian aid, the watery vast,
anchors.note: Opens the account of Menelaus's brother's fate, leading into Agamemnon's murder, matching Murray's 'thy brother escaped, indeed, the fates... for queenly Hera saved him.'

anchors.anchor: “He said: chill horrors shook my shivering soul,
anchors.note: Opens Menelaus's grief-stricken reaction to hearing of Agamemnon's murder, followed by Proteus's comfort and the eventual reveal of Odysseus's fate, matching Murray's 'any longer desire to live... when I had had my fill of weeping and writhing, then the unerring old man of the sea said to me.'

anchors.anchor: “He ceased, and plunging in the vast profound,
anchors.note: Opens the close of Proteus's revelations and Menelaus's return to his ships, matching Murray's 'So saying he plunged beneath the surging sea, but I went to my ships with my god-like comrades.'

anchors.anchor: Meanwhile, in Ithaca, the suitor powers
anchors.note: Marks the scene shift back to Ithaca and the suitors at play, matching Murray's 'the wooers in front of the palace of Odysseus were making merry, throwing the discus and the javelin.'

anchors.anchor: With vast applause the sentence all approve;
anchors.note: Follows Antinous's ambush proposal and opens the move toward Medon overhearing and warning Penelope, matching Murray's 'they all praised his words, and bade him act... Now Penelope was no long time without knowledge.'

anchors.anchor: The sage retired: unable to control
anchors.note: Marks Penelope's renewed, uncontrolled grief after Medon's departure, leading into her lament to the household and Eurycleia's confession, matching Murray's household-wide lament that opens this scene.

anchors.anchor: She ceased; shrill ecstasies of joy declare
anchors.note: Opens the goddess's favorable omen after Penelope's prayer, followed immediately by the suitors' uproar, matching Murray's 'she raised the sacred cry, and the goddess heard her prayer. But the wooers broke into uproar.'

anchors.anchor: He spoke. The god who mounts the winged winds
anchors.note: Opens Hermes's departure from Olympus after Zeus's instructions, matching Murray's 'the messenger, Argeiphontes, failed not to hearken.'

anchors.anchor: Him, entering in the cave, Calypso knew;
anchors.note: Opens Calypso's recognition of Hermes as he enters the cave, matching Murray's 'nor did Calypso, the beautiful goddess, fail to know him.'

anchors.anchor: Thus having said, he cut the cleaving sky,
anchors.note: Opens Hermes's departure and Calypso's compliant journey to find Odysseus, matching Murray's 'the strong Argeiphontes departed, and the queenly nymph went to the great-hearted Odysseus.'

anchors.anchor: Thus having said, the goddess marched before:
anchors.note: Opens the pair's walk back to the cave after Calypso's oath, matching Murray's 'the beautiful goddess led the way quickly, and he followed in the footsteps of the goddess.'

anchors.anchor: Thus while he spoke, the beamy sun descends,
anchors.note: Marks the sunset/dawn transition into the raft-building sequence, matching Murray's 'the sun set and darkness came on... As soon as early Dawn appeared, the rosy-fingered, straightway Odysseus put on a cloak and a tunic.'

anchors.anchor: Four days were pass’d, and now the work complete,
anchors.note: Opens the fourth/fifth-day formula that leads to Calypso sending him off, matching Murray's 'Now the fourth day came and all his work was done. And on the fifth the beautiful Calypso sent him on his way.'

anchors.anchor: But him, thus voyaging the deeps below,
anchors.note: Opens Poseidon's sighting of Odysseus, matching Murray's 'the glorious Earth-shaker, as he came back from the Ethiopians, beheld him from afar.'

anchors.anchor: He spoke, and high the forky trident hurl’d,
anchors.note: Marks the transition from Poseidon's internal decision to actually raising the storm winds, matching Murray's converging winds 'Together the East Wind and the South Wind dashed... the fierce-blowing West Wind and the North Wind.'

anchors.anchor: The wandering chief with toils on toils oppress’d,
anchors.note: Opens Ino/Leucothea's appearance to the storm-tossed Odysseus, matching Murray's 'the daughter of Cadmus, Ino of the fair ankles, saw him.'

anchors.anchor: While thus his thoughts an anxious council hold,
anchors.note: Opens the moment Poseidon finally destroys the raft outright, matching Murray's 'Poseidon, the earth-shaker, made to rise up a great wave, dread and grievous... and drove it upon him.'

anchors.anchor: Now, scarce withdrawn the fierce earth-shaking power,
anchors.note: Opens Athena's calming of the winds that lets Odysseus drift toward Phaeacia, matching Murray's 'she roused the swift North Wind, and broke the waves before him... Then for two nights and two days he was driven about.'

anchors.anchor: No port receives me from the angry main,
anchors.note: Redrafted after verification: murrayOpening's first clause ('nowhere doth there appear a way to come forth from the grey sea... without are sharp crags') is the start of Odysseus's despairing no-harbor/sharp-crags deliberation, not the later wave-dash; the narrator's own 'no harbor' description and the monologue's opening exclamation ('Ah me!... I have cloven a way through this gulf') both still belong to the preceding scene's span (endLine 411), so this line, where the deliberation's substance begins, is the true opening beat.

anchors.anchor: Beyond the beating surge his course he bore,
anchors.note: Opens Odysseus's swim beyond the rocks toward calmer water, matching Murray's 'Making his way forth from the surge... he swam outside, looking ever toward the land in hope to find shelving beaches and harbors.'

anchors.anchor: Now parting from the stream, Ulysses found
anchors.note: Opens Odysseus rising from the riverbank and moving on to seek shelter, matching Murray's transition into his 'Ah, woe is me!' deliberation about where to spend the night, which leads directly to the two-olive thicket.

anchors.anchor:
To his high palace through the fields of air
The goddess shot; Ulysses was her care.
anchors.note: New paragraph after the Alcinous-genealogy close ('legal sway.'); Pope's 'her care' pivots straight to Athena entering the palace, matching Murray's transition to the chamber.

anchors.anchor: Now from her rosy car Aurora shed
anchors.note: Sentence-opening dawn couplet immediately following Athena's return to Olympus, matching Murray's dawn transition before Nausicaa wakes and petitions her father.

anchors.anchor: Swift at the royal nod the attending train
anchors.note: Follows Alcinous's granting speech; this couplet begins the servants readying the mule-car, matching Murray's 'with this he called to the slaves... they made ready the wagon.'

anchors.anchor: They seek the cisterns where Phæacian dames
anchors.note: Sentence start right after the drive; matches Murray's 'Now when they came to the beautiful streams of the river, where were the washing tanks.'

anchors.anchor: Meantime (the care and favourite of the skies
anchors.note: New paragraph pivoting back to sleeping Odysseus and Pallas's plan to rouse him, matching Murray's 'the goddess...took other counsel, that Odysseus might awake.'

anchors.anchor: Then, where the grove with leaves umbrageous bends,
anchors.note: Sentence start immediately after Odysseus's lament ends with a question mark; matches Murray's 'he broke from the thick wood a leafy branch.'

anchors.anchor: But fearful to offend, by wisdom sway’d,
anchors.note: Sentence start capping Odysseus's deliberation, matching Murray's 'it seemed to him better to stand apart and beseech her with gentle words... so straightway he spoke.'

anchors.anchor: To whom the nymph: “O stranger, cease thy care;
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Odysseus's supplication ends; matches Murray's 'Then white-armed Nausicaa answered him: Stranger, since thou seemest...'

anchors.anchor: To them the king: “No longer I detain
anchors.note: Sentence start where Odysseus asks the maids to withdraw so he can bathe, matching Murray's 'Then among the maidens spoke goodly Odysseus: Maidens, stand yonder apart.'

anchors.anchor: The wondering nymph his glorious port survey’d,
anchors.note: Sentence start after Odysseus reclines by the shore, matching Murray's 'the damsel marvelled at him, and spoke to her fair-tressed handmaids.'

anchors.anchor: Now on return her care Nausicaa bends,
anchors.note: Sentence start after Odysseus eats his fill; matches Murray's 'the white-armed Nausicaa took other counsel... mounted the car herself... hailed Odysseus.'

anchors.anchor: But would’st thou soon review thy native plain?
anchors.note: Pope renders Nausicaa's whole speech as one unbroken quotation, so this scene opens mid-speech; this line is the nearest topical pivot to the escort-home/grove/Arete instructions (matching Murray's 'thou mayest win from my father an escort and a return to thy land'), though Pope punctuates the preceding line with a comma rather than a period.

anchors.anchor: She added not, but waving, as she wheel’d,
anchors.note: Sentence start immediately after Nausicaa's speech closes; matches Murray's 'So saying, she smote the mules with the shining whip.'

anchors.anchor: Now from the sacred thicket where he lay,
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after the Eurymedusa digression closes; matches Murray's 'Odysseus roused himself to go to the city, and Athena...cast [a mist about him].'

anchors.anchor: When near the famed Phæacian walls he drew,
anchors.note: Sentence start (previous line ends 'loud.') containing the actual meeting ('His step a virgin met, and stood before'), matching Murray's disguised maiden standing before him.

anchors.anchor: Thus having spoke, the unknown celestial leads:
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start after the girl's warning speech closes; matches Murray's 'the Phaeacians...took no heed of him, for...Athena...shed about him a wondrous mist,' immediately followed by his wonder at the city and her genealogy speech and departure to Athens, all within this scene's line range.

anchors.anchor: Meanwhile Ulysses at the palace waits,
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Athena's departure to Athens closes the prior scene; matches Murray's arrival 'over the high-roofed house of great-hearted Alcinous' and the ensuing bronze-wall description.

anchors.anchor: Such were the glories which the gods ordain’d,
anchors.note: Sentence start closing the palace-description catalogue, echoing Murray's 'Such were the glorious gifts of the gods in the palace of Alcinous,' immediately followed by his entering the hall.

anchors.anchor: Then from around him dropp’d the veil of night;
anchors.note: Sentence start where the concealing mist drops and he is seen, matching Murray's transition into his prayer to Arete.

anchors.anchor: Then to the genial hearth he bow’d his face,
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Odysseus's supplication speech closes; matches Murray's 'he sat down on the hearth in the ashes by the fire...Echeneus' speaking up.

anchors.anchor: Thus feasting high, Alcinous gave the sign,
anchors.note: Sentence start (previous line ends 'repast!') introducing the libation command, matching Murray's fragment on pouring libations to Zeus before Alcinous addresses the assembly.

anchors.anchor: “Let no such thought (with modest grace rejoin’d
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start immediately after Alcinous's speech on possible divine guests ends; matches Murray's 'Then Odysseus of many wiles answered him...for I am not like the immortals.'

anchors.anchor: The assembled peers with general praise approved
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start after Odysseus's plea to eat and depart at dawn ends; matches Murray's 'they all praised his words...went each man to his home...Odysseus was left behind...beside him sat Arete and Alcinous.'

anchors.anchor: “Hard is the task, O princess! you impose
anchors.note: Direct-speech opening right after Arete's question about his robe and origin closes; matches Murray's 'Then Odysseus of many wiles answered her...Hard were it, O queen, to tell to the end the tale of my woes.'

anchors.anchor: To this the king: “Our daughter but express’d
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Odysseus finishes his narrative; matches Murray's 'Alcinous answered him...verily my daughter was not minded aright in this.'

anchors.anchor: Thus he. No word the experienced man replies,
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start after Alcinous's boast about his ships closes; matches Murray's 'the much-enduring goodly Odysseus was glad; and he spoke in prayer.'

anchors.anchor: She spoke, and sudden with tumultuous sounds
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after the herald's summons ends; matches Murray's 'she roused the spirit and heart of each man...the place of assembly...were filled.'

anchors.anchor: Thus spoke the prince; the attending peers obey;
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Alcinous's proposal speech ends; matches Murray's 'he led the way, and the sceptred kings followed him, while a herald went for the divine minstrel.'

anchors.anchor: Then, fired by all the Muse, aloud he sings
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start after the feast is served; matches Murray's 'the Muse moved the minstrel to sing...even the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles.'

anchors.anchor: Transported with the song, the listening train
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start describing renewed applause and Odysseus again veiling his tears; matches Murray's 'Alcinous alone marked him and took heed...he sat by him, and heard him groaning heavily.'

anchors.anchor: Thus spoke the king; the attending peers obey;
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Alcinous's games proposal closes; matches Murray's 'he led the way, and they followed him' as they proceed to the games.

anchors.anchor: To whom with sighs Ulysses gave reply:
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Laodamas/Euryalus's persuasion speech ends ('stretch the swelling sails'); matches Murray's 'Then Odysseus of many wiles answered him, and said: Laodamas, why do ye mock me.' (The taunt/rebuke named in the summary follows later in this same scene.)

anchors.anchor: Then gliding forward with a furious bound
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Odysseus's angry rebuke to Euryalus closes ('slander stings the brave'); matches Murray's 'He spoke, and, leaping up with his cloak about him...seized a discus.'

anchors.anchor: Abash’d, the numbers hear the godlike man,
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Odysseus's bow-boasting speech ends; matches Murray's 'they were all hushed in silence; but Alcinous alone answered him.'

anchors.anchor: Meantime the bard, alternate to the strings,
anchors.note: Sentence start right after the dancers' sandals are described; matches Murray's 'the minstrel struck the chords in prelude to his sweet lay and sang of the love of Ares and Aphrodite,' the scene's core action.

anchors.anchor: Then to the sports his sons the king commands,
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after the Ares/Aphrodite song ends; matches Murray's 'Alcinous bade Halius and Laodamas dance alone...taken in their hands the beautiful ball.'

anchors.anchor: Pleas’d with his people’s fame, the monarch hears,
anchors.note: Sentence/paragraph start right after Odysseus's praise of Phaeacian skill ends; matches Murray's 'Alcinous was glad; and straightway he spoke...Come then, let us give him a gift of friendship.'

anchors.anchor: Instant the queen, observant of the king,

anchors.anchor: To whom, while anger in his bosom glows,

anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'He spoke, and made the many falsehoods of his tale seem like the truth, and as she listened her tears flowed.'

anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Then Odysseus of many wiles answered her, and said: "Honored wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, mar not now thy fair face any more."'

anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Then wise Penelope answered him: "Ah, stranger, I would that this word of thine might be fulfilled."'

anchors.anchor: Instant, obsequious to the mild command,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'So she spoke, and the old woman hid her face in her hands and let fall hot tears, uttering words of lamentation: "Ah, woe is me, child."'

anchors.anchor: Deep o’er his knee inseam’d remain’d the scar;
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'This scar the old dame, when she had taken the limb in the flat of her hands, knew by the touch, and she let fall the foot.'

anchors.anchor: Then thus rejoin’d the dame, devoid of fear:
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Then wise Eurycleia answered him: "My child, what a word has escaped the barrier of thy teeth!"'

anchors.anchor: Adjusting to his limbs the tatter’d vest,
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'And when she had washed him, and anointed him richly with oil, Odysseus again drew his chair nearer to the fire... Then wise Penelope was the first to speak.'

anchors.anchor: A visionary thought I’ll now relate;
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'But come now, hear this dream of mine, and interpret it for me. Twenty geese I have in the house.'

anchors.anchor: “Hard is the task, and rare,” (the queen rejoin’d,)
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'Then wise Penelope answered him again: "Stranger, dreams verily are baffling and unclear of meaning."'

anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the spirit of the son of Atreus answered him: Happy son of Laertes'.

anchors.note: Directly renders Murray's 'Laertes answered him again... tell me now some clear sign'.

anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'they sprang up with loud cries, more than half of them' opening the scene.

anchors.anchor: This pass’d on earth, while in the realms above
anchors.note: Directly renders Murray's 'Athena spoke to Zeus, son of Cronos, saying' opening the scene.

anchors.anchor: Now sat Ulysses at the rural feast
anchors.note: Matches Murray's 'the much-enduring, goodly Odysseus was the first to speak among his company' opening the scene.
